title: How to Play Openings
transcript: How to play the opening properly? Well, why don't we have a look at one of your games, unknown person? This is day six of reviewing one of my followers' games every single day until I hit 100,000 followers. If you want me to review your game, all you have to do is like this video, follow me, and comment your chess.com username. So, you open up with the F3 knight. This is called the Reti Opening. Now, at this level, I would suggest you very closely follow these three opening principles: control the center, then develop your pieces, and then bring the king to safety. So, pick a move between E4 or D4 as your first move to control the center. Now, this is still fine. You control the center on the next move, but you really, really want to get used with internalizing the opening principles. Now, we always want to be aware of what is being attacked. In this case, the pawn is being attacked, and the knight is being attacked. And it's important to realize that the only defender of the pawn is this knight. So, black is threatening to take the knight, and once you take back, the bishop they're going to take the pawn, which means that in this position, this pawn is threatened. Now, whenever something is under attack, there are three ways to get out of it. You can either remove the attacking piece, which we cannot do in this case. The attacking piece is the knight. You can defend the attacked piece, which we can do. It might not be ideal, because if you open up here, now there is a permanent pin on this knight. Or we can move the attacked piece, and that is the best option here. You can simply push the pawn. Now, if black jumps to the center, you can take and damage their pawn structure. And if black were to take this knight, do not take their knight, because they can come back with the bishop, and now be up a pawn. Instead, we take here, we open up the queen, and now their knight has to move. Once it does, we can attack it again, and now you're getting a pretty significant advantage. Instead, you develop your bishop, and I feel like this is kind of an autopilot move. You just want to develop your pieces and castle, which is a good instinct, but you also have to acknowledge what your opponent is trying to do. And so, after this move, you're just going to lose a pawn in the center. Now, here you castle, which I like, and your opponent attacks the bishop. You play this move, D3, trying to counterattack the knight. In principle, this makes sense, but it is always a little bit trickier to play these moves rather than simply save your bishop. This would be the simplest option. Whereas after this move, you now have to take into consideration all of those moves that get out of the threat. And your opponent finds a very good move here, knight to C3, counterattacking the queen while still attacking the bishop and winning a pawn. Also important to remember that every single pawn push leaves a weakness behind, in this case, the C pawn. And it is very important to acknowledge what our opponents are attacking in our side of the board, especially when a piece is this close to our pieces. And well, that's how we see that the queen is under attack, which unfortunately, you miss, and you lose the queen on the next move and resign the game. Bonus tip, stop playing these many bullet games. You are now officially in bullet jail. Focus on rapid.
